Second Commandment
SEK-uhnd kuh-MAND-muhnt
noun phrase (commandment)
The second word of the Decalogue (Exo 20:4-6): the prohibition of graven images and of worship by means of them — governing not WHOM we worship (the first commandment) but HOW.

Biblical Definition

The second commandment is the second word of the Decalogue: 'Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image... thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God' (Exo 20:4-5). Where the first commandment fixes the OBJECT of worship — no other gods — the second governs its MANNER: the true God must not be worshiped by images or by any means of man's devising. Moses presses the ground of it: at Horeb 'ye saw no manner of similitude' (Deut 4:15) — God revealed Himself by His word, not by a form, and to manufacture a form is to exchange His glory for a likeness and inevitably to shrink Him. The golden calf proves the commandment's edge: Aaron did not announce a new god but proclaimed 'a feast to the LORD' (Exo 32:5) — Israel was worshiping YHWH by an image, and the LORD counted it apostasy. From this commandment the Reformed churches drew the regulative principle of worship — God is to be worshiped only as He has appointed in His Word — and, with the historic Reformed confessions, declined to make images of God in any person, the Lord Jesus included, since no image can show what He is: 'God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth' (John 4:24). The commandment carries a promise as wide as its threat: mercy unto thousands of them that love Him and keep His commandments.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Decalogue's second word (Exo 20:4-6): the true God must not be worshiped by images or man-devised means — the golden calf was a 'feast to the LORD' and yet apostasy; the root of the regulative principle of worship.

SECOND COMMANDMENT, noun phrase. Exodus 20:4-6: no graven images; no bowing to them.

Governs the MANNER of worship, as the first commandment governs its OBJECT.

Grounded at Horeb: 'ye saw no manner of similitude' (Deut 4:15).

Proved at the golden calf: worship of the LORD by an image is apostasy (Exo 32:5).

The root of the regulative principle: God worshiped only as His Word appoints.

Key Scripture

Exo 20:4 — "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:"

Exo 20:5 — "Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;"

Deut 4:15 — "Take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves; for ye saw no manner of similitude on the day that the LORD spake unto you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire:"

John 4:24 — "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth."

Modern Corruption

The second commandment is corrupted when it is collapsed into the first (as Rome's numbering does, hiding it), when images are defended as 'aids' to devotion, and when worship is governed by what feels authentic rather than what God has appointed.

expand to see more

Image-as-aid misreading. The perennial defense — from the calf to the medieval church — is that the image is not the god, only a help to worship Him. The commandment forecloses exactly this: Aaron's calf was offered as a feast TO THE LORD (Exo 32:5), and God judged it as rebellion, because every manufactured likeness lies about the God who showed no similitude and shrinks His glory to the measure of the craftsman. The dictionary holds, with the historic Reformed confessions, that the true God is not to be imaged in any person — and that He has given His own appointed pictures: the Word, the water, the bread and the cup.

Authenticity-worship misreading. The modern form of the corruption rarely carves idols; it enthrones the worshiper, governing worship by what feels moving, expressive, or authentic to the self. But the second commandment locates the rule of worship in God's appointment, not man's invention — the regulative principle: what He has not commanded for His worship, He has forbidden. The dictionary commends the freedom in this: worship by God's appointment is worship He has promised to bless, and the conscience is freed from every device of men.

Hebrew Roots

The Decalogue's second word: no images, no man-devised worship — the manner of worship belongs to God's appointment; root of the regulative principle, proved at the golden calf.

Usage

"The second commandment — not WHOM we worship but HOW: by God's appointment, not man's image."

"Ye saw no manner of similitude (Deut 4:15) — the ground of the second commandment."

"The golden calf was a feast to the LORD by an image — and God counted it apostasy (Exo 32:5)."
